notes.meaning: Praising the Lord is both good and delightful. Singing to God is the right response for those who belong to him, and it brings joy to the worshiper. Giving him honor fits who he is and what he has done.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine taught that praise cannot just come from the tongue for a short time; a person's entire life and conduct must offer praise to God.

notes.meaning: The Lord rebuilds the ruined city of Jerusalem and brings his scattered people back home from exile. Even when his people seem hopelessly dispersed, God knows where they are and gathers them. His work of restoring his people cannot be stopped.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine interpreted Jerusalem as the heavenly city, teaching that humanity was scattered by sin and gathered back by Christ through his blood.

notes.meaning: God tenderly heals those whose hearts are crushed by sorrow or grief over sin. He bandages their deep emotional wounds like a caring doctor. While he governs whole nations, he also attends to the personal pain of every hurting person.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine viewed the brokenhearted as the humble, whom God bandages in this life through the church, the scriptures, and the sacraments until full healing comes in heaven.

notes.meaning: God decides the exact number of the stars and calls each one by its own name. Because he keeps track of every light in the vast sky, he can easily locate and care for every one of his scattered people. Nothing about us is lost or hidden from him.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine saw the stars as faithful believers in the church whose names are recorded to reign with God in heaven.

notes.meaning: The Lord possesses great power, and his understanding has no limit. Human beings can never measure his deep wisdom or count all that he knows. We can trust him fully because he knows every problem and has the strength to solve it.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine noted that while God can number all the stars, his own wisdom is infinite and beyond any number.

notes.meaning: The Lord lifts up the humble and afflicted who depend on him. At the same time, he brings down the wicked and humbles their pride. God will always vindicate those who rely on his help.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine explained that the wicked thrown down are the fierce and arrogant who refuse to become gentle.

notes.meaning: Worshipers are invited to sing out their thanks to God and accompany their voices with the harp. In ancient times, this often meant taking turns singing verses back and forth. Making joyful music is a fitting way to celebrate God's goodness.

God gathers clouds in the sky, prepares rain for the earth, and makes fresh grass grow on high hills. The weather is not an accident but part of his daily rule over nature. He uses clouds and showers to bring food out of the soil.

God provides food for wild animals and answers the cries of young ravens. If he cares for needy creatures that humans often overlook, he will certainly take care of his people. We can rely on him to meet our daily needs.

God does not rely on the strength of powerful war horses, nor is he impressed by the speed and stamina of human soldiers. Armies and physical might cannot bring true rescue on their own. Victory and safety come from God rather than bodily power.

The Lord takes delight in people who honor him with reverence and place their hope in his faithful love. He values humble trust far more than human boasting or self-reliance. Our confidence belongs in his unchanging mercy.

Jerusalem and Mount Zion are called out by name to praise their God. The city that received God's special protection owed him great thanksgiving. God's people should be the first to speak well of his name.

God makes the city gates secure against enemies and pours out his blessing on the children living inside. Strong bolts and walls only work because the Lord himself is protecting the community. Real safety for families comes from his hand.

The Lord protects the borders of the land so his people can live in peace without fear of attack. He also feeds them generously with the very finest wheat. He gives both security from outside dangers and plenty of food at home.

God sends out his order to the earth, and his word travels quickly like a royal runner. Everything in nature obeys him at once, without delay or resistance. His spoken command has total authority over all things.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine interpreted God sending his Word to the earth as the arrival of Christ to save fallen humanity.

notes.meaning: God spreads snow across the ground like a white blanket of wool and sprinkles frost like fine ashes. Snow blankets the soil, helping to shield plant roots from bitter cold. Even winter weather carries out his good purposes.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine saw the snow as an image of humanity grown cold in sin, among whom God's chosen people are found.

notes.meaning: God throws down hail and ice like pieces of broken crumbs. When he sends severe winter cold, no one can endure it without his mercy. This intense weather shows how small humans are compared to God's mighty power.

God speaks a simple command, and the freezing ice melts away. He causes a warm wind to blow, and frozen waters begin flowing freely again. In the same way, God can easily thaw cold, hard hearts by the warmth of his Spirit.

God revealed his laws, teachings, and spoken word directly to Israel. While all nations could see his work in nature, only Israel received the scriptures showing his will and character. Having God's truth was their greatest blessing.

The Lord did not give his written laws and covenants to any other nation at that time. Israel received a unique privilege, which brought a special duty to know and obey him. This great goodness calls for a final shout of praise to the Lord.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine taught that what was uniquely revealed to Israel was that righteous people are saved by the free grace of God, not by their own merits.
